extracted.intended_audience: physicians, medical students, and hospital pharmacists performing clinical chemical analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and interpretive guidance for clinical chemical analysis of body fluids (especially urine) for use by physicians, students and pharmacists; includes sampling, instrumental measurement, gravimetric assays (extrait sec, cendres), and interpretation of physical signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling for qualitative vs quantitative urine analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative tests: prefer the night urine collected in the morning (fasting) for qualitative assays. Quantitative tests: collect urine over a 24-hour period and perform assays on the mixed 24‑hour specimen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one intends a qualitative assay, test the night urine collected on awakening before food or drink. For quantitative determinations results must be related to the total 24-hour urine and not simply expressed per liter, because instantaneous urine volumes vary greatly during the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure urine density with a urometer (pèse-urines / uromètre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small densimeter (uromètre) floated in an almost full vessel of urine, removing foam beforehand; read the graduating on the stem at the plane of the liquid surface (AB), avoiding reading at the meniscus summit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instrument is calibrated so distilled water corresponds to 1000; small urometers often mark only the two last digits. Immerse the clean urometer so it floats freely without touching the vessel wall and set the eye level to the liquid surface to read the division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature correction for urometer readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Most urine densimeters are graduated for 15°C; their readings are only exact when the urine is at that temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clinical purposes use the rule: a 5°C difference corresponds approximately to 1 unit on the densimeter. Add 1 to the read number for each 5°C the urine is above 15°C, subtract 1 for each 5°C below 15°C. Measure urine temperature with a thermometer placed in the urine and wait until stable. Note: this correction is valid only for near-normal urines and may be inaccurate for very dense pathologic urines (eg, glycosuric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of urometers with internal thermometer / design notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some urometers include an internal thermometer (thermometer bulb forming the ballast) to facilitate simultaneous density and temperature measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined instruments simplify taking both values; nonetheless, ensure the instrument is clean and that readings are taken at the liquid surface plane, not at the meniscus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of dry residue (extrait sec) of urine (gravimetric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain the dry residue by evaporating a measured aliquot (standard: 10 c.c.) to dryness in a platinum capsule, then heat in an oven at 100°C for one hour, cool under a desiccator (acid sulphuric or quicklime), and weigh repeatedly until constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust sample volume by density: if urine density ≤ 1.010 use 20 c.c.; if ≥ 1.030 use 5 c.c. Remove foam before evaporating. Repeat heating/cooling/weighing cycles (usually 2–3 hours total) until weight is constant. Deduct capsule tare to obtain residue per aliquot and then express per litre or per 24 hours as required. Protect the residue from atmospheric moisture during weighing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for glucose effect on dry residue (Méhu double-extract control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In glycosuric urines urea decomposes during oven drying and causes progressive weight loss of the residue; to correct, Méhu recommends performing the dry residue in duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce dry extracts in two identical capsules. After extensive dessiccation, weigh the residues, re-dissolve one in distilled water to original urine volume and determine urea in that solution to estimate urea lost by decomposition; add the lost urea weight to the first capsule's residue. Use the second capsule as a control of the operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most exact dry residue method (Maguier de la Source vacuum evaporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most accurate procedure is to evaporate 1–2 grams of urine in vacuum in presence of concentrated sulphuric acid, which achieves dessiccation in about 24 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This vacuum method avoids urea decomposition and provides precise dry residue values but requires appropriate apparatus and concentrated H2SO4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical estimation of dry residue from density (Apollinaire Boucliardat rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An approximate clinic-friendly method: double the last two digits of the urometer reading to estimate grams of dry residue per litre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: urometer 1.022 → last two digits 22 → double → 44 g/L. This approximation is reasonably accurate for normal urine but deviates for pathological urines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of urinary ash (cendres) and precautions to avoid chloride loss
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine mineral ash, incinerate the dry extract in platinum but avoid direct high-temperature incineration that volatilizes chlorides and reduces sulfates and phosphates; perform the operation in two steps with careful carbonization, aqueous extraction of soluble salts, filtration and controlled calcination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: gently char the residue (lamp) until organic matter is carbonized; cool, add hot distilled water, triturate and filter to recover soluble salts (which should be incolor). Concentrate the filtrate and keep aside. Calcine the filter and char residue in the platinum capsule with a Bunsen to complete incineration; use ammonium nitrate or ammonium-urea solution during calcination to aid combustion (recognize this introduces azotates that overweigh ash). To reverse azotates to carbonates use a small fragment of stearic acid and reheat. Finally combine re-evaporated soluble fraction and incinerated ashes, dry carefully (avoid splintering losses) and weigh to obtain cendres of the urine per aliquot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate heating and handling to avoid analytical errors (ash and residue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct high-temperature incineration of urinary residue gives erroneous ash weights because chlorides volatilize and organic carbon reduces sulfates/phosphates releasing volatile phosphorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence the two-step gentle carbonization, aqueous extraction and careful calcination described above. During final drying prefer low heat (B.M. or oven at 100°C) then finish on an alcohol lamp; cool under desiccator and weigh quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction (acid/alkaline) testing using litmus papers and 'purple' litmus
rubrics_metrics.description: Urine is normally acidic (reaction due mainly to sodium acid phosphate); use litmus paper (blue→red in acid; red→blue in alkaline). Prepared 'purple' litmus that reddens in acid and blues in alkaline is convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alkalinity may be produced transiently by alkali ingestion or an exclusively vegetable diet; also urine becomes alkaline after standing due to urease activity. For accurate assessment examine urine shortly after emission. Neutral urine does not change litmus tint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermentation (urease) effect and urgency of testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Urine left standing undergoes ammoniacal fermentation (urea→ammonium carbonate) under action of urease from microbes (notably Micrococcus ureæ), making urine alkaline and producing deposits; this process is faster with high temperature or when urine contains blood, albumin or pus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine urine soon after emission. An alkaline urine already upon leaving the bladder is worrisome clinically. Albuminous/purulent urines may acid at micturition and soon become alkaline; thus timing matters for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of urine colour as clinical sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal urine is amber-yellow; colour varies with time, concentration, disease, and ingested substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pale/incolor urine indicates low solids and low density (except in diabetic glycosuria). Dark urine usually indicates concentration and higher solids. Yellow-green indicates bile pigments (icteric urine). Red/brown by blood (neoplasm, nephritis, cystitis) or hemoglobinuria; black in decomposition or melanotic cancer; drugs (senna, rhubarb, phenol, tar) can also change colour. Colour may deepen on aeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of urine odour
rubrics_metrics.description: Urine has a sui generis odour which varies with foods, drugs and disease; some volatiles impart characteristic smells (eg, turpentine → violet odor; asparagus → fetid odor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infectious or purulent conditions (pus, stones, cancer) can render urine fetid. Note odour changes and consider recent ingestion of odour-producing substances or exposures when interpreting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and foam as diagnostic indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal urine is as fluid as water and makes little transient foam; increased foam that is more abundant and persistent suggests blood, pus or albumin. Putrefaction of pus in urine yields viscous, stringy 'filante' consistency and alkaline reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe agitation-induced foam and viscosity; correlate with other findings (microscopy, reagents) to distinguish causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/turbidity and its causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal urine is limpid but a slight cloud may form soon after emission from mucus and epithelial debris. Immediate turbidity at emission usually indicates pathology (pus, phosphates/carbonates deposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clouding that appears on cooling is due to precipitation of urates, oxalates, or pigments. 'Jumenteuse' (horse-like) turbid urine indicates heavy phosphate deposition typical of some conditions. Differentiate immediate turbidity (pathologic) from delayed precipitates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity (24-hour urine volume) clinical norms and extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report urine volume over 24 hours: adult male average ~1400–1500 c.c.; female somewhat lower (~1100–1200 c.c.); values vary with weight, age, diet, exercise and temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect over 24 hours for accurate quantification. Pathologic states may reduce secretion to 100–150 c.c. per 24h or increase it to 6–20 L (or even 25–30 L in diabetes insipidus). Instantaneous samples are misleading for quantitative interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference values and ranges for urine density
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean urine density in healthy adults: ~1.018 (men) and ~1.016 (women), with typical range 1.014–1.028. Polyuric urine may be ~1.001, diabetic urine may reach 1.030–1.070.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the urometer to obtain density; interpret values in clinical context (volume, glucose, protein) and consider temperature corrections and limits of gravimetric corrections in pathologic samples.
